newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel prepares for Hebron redeployment.
newsitem.headline: Israel prepares for Hebron redeployment.

text.p: Soldiers hauled away sentry boxes and the fixtures of 30 years of occupation on Thursday, ahead of the green light from Israel's parliament to transfer Hebron to Palestinian rule.
Only a handful of Palestinians watched in stinging rain as one soldier pulled down a blue-and-white Star of David flag from an army checkpoint at the entrance to the West Bank city.
Army commanders said the full-scale redeployment agreed on Wednesday between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat had not yet begun.

They were waiting for word from Jerusalem where parliament began debating the U.S.-brokered accord that has split Netanyahu's centre-right coalition. The cabinet approved the deal by 11 votes to seven in a stormy 12-hour session ending early on Thursday.

The deal, which allows Israel to stay in one fifth of Hebron, is expected to easily pass in the Knesset with the support of the Labour opposition that signed the first self-rule deal with Arafat in 1993.

Paratroopers in red berets fanned out through Hebron to cover those removing equipment and prevent protests by Jewish settlers against the agreement. Other soldiers and police set up makeshift roadblocks.
"The removal of the equipment does not change any decision," Major-General Gabi Ofir told army radio. "We are remaining in our usual deployment and on the contrary, have even reinforced our presence.
"But at the same time we are removing some of the equipment and if it is indeed decided we should redeploy, we will keep any timetable necessary."
Palestinian officials said 400 civilian and paramilitary police were poised to take over.
"As soon as the redeployment begins, our forces are ready to enter the city," Hebron commander Brigadier-General Abdel-Fattah al-Jaidi told Reuters.
Palestinian police have been discreetly bringing vehicles and equipment into Hebron for months with Israel's knowledge.
Israeli cranes plucked steel sentry boxes from rooftops and rain-drenched conscripts dragged away the paraphenalia of an occupation that began before they were born.
They split open sand bags, pulled down barbed wire and dismantled search lights. A washstand too big to pass through a door was poked through one barrack-room window.
"We're very happy to see them go," said Hamed Khalil Amr, watching from his butcher shop. "We hope the settlers will do the same thing and leave our town and let us live in peace."

Some 400 militant settlers live in the heart of Hebron. Another 5,000 live in fenced enclaves on the edge of this city of 100,000 Palestinians that contains the tomb of the biblical Abraham, a site revered by Jews and Moslems.
"It's a sad day when a Jewish government takes this very grave decision," settler Moshe Ben-Zimra said.
"Netanyahu will be remembered as the first prime minister who abandoned the legacy of the fathers to outsiders, who abandoned Jewish lives in the Land of Israel," he said.

Hebron is the last of seven West Bank towns Israel agreed to transfer to Palestinians under their peace agreement. The status of East Jerusalem, the biggest West Bank Palestinian city, is to be negotiated by 1999, after three further Israeli withdrawals from rural areas.

The wrangling inside Netanyahu's cabinet reflected the deep split in the Likud-led coalition over ceding land to Palestinians that many Israelis believe to be theirs by biblical right. Science Minister Binyamin Begin, son of the late prime minister Menachem Begin, resigned over the agreement.

But an opinion poll in Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper said 67 percent of Israelis were pleased with the Hebron deal. In response to another question, 80 percent of the 504 people polled said they had not visited Hebron in the last five years.
